blocks.text: **The problem.** You're given a doubly linked list whose nodes also have a **child** pointer. A child pointer, when it isn't null, leads to a separate doubly linked list — a lower **level** — whose nodes may have children of their own. **Flatten** the structure into one doubly linked list: each child level goes **right after its parent node**, before the parent's old next. Set every `child` to null and return the head.

blocks.alt: Three levels. The top level is 1, 2, 3, 4. Node 3 has a child level 7, 8, 9 drawn below it, and node 8 has a child level 11, 12 below that. Flattened, each child level is inserted right after its parent: 1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 11, 12, 9, 4.

blocks.text: The flattened order is a **depth-first** walk: visit a node, then (if it has one) its **whole child level** — including that level's own children — and only then the node's old next. It's the same order as a pre-order traversal of a tree where `child` is the first branch and `next` the second.

Three ways to produce it: collect the nodes in that order and relink them; use an explicit **stack** (push `next`, then `child`, so the child comes out first); or **splice** each child level into place as you walk, which needs no extra memory at all.
1. Collect the nodes in order, then relink

blocks.code:
def flatten(head):
    order = []

    def visit(node):                      # node, then its child level, then the rest
        while node is not None:
            order.append(node)
            if node.child is not None:
                visit(node.child)
            node = node.next

    visit(head)
    for i, node in enumerate(order):      # relink everything in that order
        node.prev = order[i - 1] if i > 0 else None
        node.next = order[i + 1] if i + 1 < len(order) else None
        node.child = None
    return head

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(n)** for the array of nodes (plus the recursion, as deep as the number of levels). Simple and safe: the links are only rewritten after the walk has finished reading them.
2. A stack: next waits while the child goes first

**Time O(n), space O(d)**, where d is the depth of nesting — each level leaves one `next` waiting on the stack. Pushing `next` before `child` is the whole trick: a stack pops the last thing pushed first.
3. Splice each child level in place

blocks.caption: Find the child level's tail, join it to curr's old next, then hang the level after curr.

blocks.code:
def flatten(head):
    curr = head
    while curr is not None:
        if curr.child is not None:
            tail = curr.child
            while tail.next is not None:  # the end of the child level
                tail = tail.next
            tail.next = curr.next         # child level's tail -> curr's old next
            if curr.next is not None:
                curr.next.prev = tail
            curr.next = curr.child        # curr -> the child level
            curr.child.prev = curr
            curr.child = None
        curr = curr.next                  # the spliced level is walked next
    return head

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(1).** After a splice, `curr` walks straight into the child level, so deeper children are spliced when it reaches them — that keeps the depth-first order. Each node is passed once by `curr` and at most once by a tail search, because it belongs to exactly one level.

blocks.alt: Collect, then relink: O(n) time, O(n) space. Stack: O(n) time, O(depth) space. Splice in place: O(n) time, O(1) space.

blocks.text: The stack version is the usual first answer and is easy to get right. The splice version is the one to aim for: it uses the doubly linked pointers themselves as the only bookkeeping.

items: **No children** — the list comes back unchanged.
**A child on the last node** — its level becomes the new end; nothing comes after its tail.
**Nested children** — 3 has a child level whose node 8 has its own child: 8's level must come before the rest of 3's level.
**Forgetting `child = null` or a `prev`** — the result must be a clean doubly linked list: every `prev` correct and every `child` null.
**Flatten a multilevel list level by level** — breadth-first instead: append each child level to the **end** of the list as you meet it.
**Flatten Binary Tree to Linked List** — the same pre-order splice, with `left` as the child and `right` as next.
**Copy List with Random Pointer** — another list with an extra pointer per node; interleave copies to use O(1) extra space.
